opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, that's a great question, and it's really at the heart of how I think about self-supervised learning.

The way I like to frame it is that an embedding is only as meaningful as the objective that shaped it. When you train a model on raw signal, say video or images, you're implicitly making a choice about what information you want the representation to keep and what you're happy to throw away. With generative or reconstruction-based approaches, where you predict pixels, the model is pushed to hold on to everything: textures, lighting, high-frequency noise, details that are fundamentally unpredictable. A lot of the model's capacity goes into modeling things that, for most downstream tasks, you don't actually care about.

With joint-embedding predictive architectures, the JEPA family, the idea is to make the prediction in representation space instead. You take part of the signal, encode it, and try to predict the representation of another part, maybe a masked region or a future frame. Because you're predicting embeddings rather than pixels, the model is free to discard what isn't predictable and focus on what is: the structure, the semantics, how objects move and interact. So the embedding ends up containing the predictable, abstract information about the scene, and that tends to be what's useful for understanding, and eventually for planning.

There's a caveat, of course. If you're not careful, the easiest way to make embeddings predictable is to make them constant, so you get collapse. A lot of the engineering in these methods, things like the asymmetric target encoder with an exponential moving average, or how you design the masking, exists to keep the representation informative while still being predictable.

In practice, I think about it empirically, too. We probe the embeddings: frozen-backbone evaluations, linear or attentive probes on tasks like action recognition or object classification, or checking whether a world model built on top can actually be used to plan. That tells you what's linearly accessible in the representation. But I'd say the deeper intuition is that the embedding reflects your choice of what's worth predicting. Get that choice right and the representation captures the stuff about the world that matters.

r001.rationale: The response says embeddings should focus on structure and semantics, and describes them as containing predictable, abstract information. It does not state that embeddings need not perform semantic abstraction.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the way I think about it is that an embedding is really a kind of abstraction of the input. When you take an image, say, there's an enormous amount of information in that image. You've got the exact pixel values, the texture of the grass, the lighting, the little bit of noise from the camera sensor. And a lot of that, honestly, is not something you'd ever want to predict, and it's not something you'd ever need to predict to do most of the things you care about.

So when you're learning from a signal, the question becomes: what do you want the embedding to retain, and what do you want it to throw away? And the beautiful thing about learning in embedding space, as opposed to reconstructing pixels, is that the model gets to make that decision. If you train the model to predict the embedding of some part of the input from the embedding of another part, the model is incentivized to keep the information that's actually predictable, the semantic structure, the identity of objects, their rough positions, how things relate to each other, and it's free to discard the stuff that's fundamentally unpredictable, like the exact noise pattern or the precise texture of every blade of grass.

So I don't really think of an embedding as containing the input. I think of it as containing a particular view of the input, shaped by the prediction task. And that's actually a feature, not a bug. The whole point is that you want a representation where the things that matter are easy to read off and the things that don't matter are gone.

Now, the flip side is that this makes it really important how you set up the learning problem, because the embedding will only contain what the objective encourages it to contain. If the task is too easy, the embedding can collapse, it can keep almost nothing and still solve the task. If the task doesn't require understanding the world, the embedding won't understand the world. So a lot of what we spend our time on is designing the prediction problem so that the only way to solve it is to actually capture the structure that we care about. And then the embeddings end up being these pretty useful, pretty general objects that you can build on top of for downstream tasks without ever having told the model what those tasks were going to be.

r001.rationale: The candidate says an embedding is “a kind of abstraction” and describes retaining semantic structure, so it does not state that embeddings need not perform semantic abstraction.

astra-6.text:
I think of an embedding as a representation of the input that preserves some information and throws away other information. The interesting question is: what do you keep? Because that’s really determined by the objective you use to learn that representation.

If you’re learning from images, for example, you might want two views of the same object to have similar representations, even if the lighting or the background changes. That encourages the model to preserve information about the object and become less sensitive to those other details. But those details could matter for a different task, so there isn’t one universally correct set of information for an embedding to contain.

And the information doesn’t necessarily live in neatly interpretable coordinates, where one dimension corresponds to one concept. It can be distributed across the representation. So I tend to think about what you can predict from an embedding, and how easily you can predict it. That gives you a more useful handle on what the model has actually learned.

r001.rationale: The response says embeddings preserve or discard information according to the learning objective and may lack interpretable coordinates. It does not state that embeddings need not perform semantic abstraction of the encoded signal.

sol-6.1.text:
I think of an embedding as a representation of the signal that preserves some information and discards other information. The important question is: what does the learning objective encourage it to preserve? You don’t necessarily want to retain every detail of the input. You want to retain the information that helps you understand the underlying structure and make useful predictions.

So, for example, with an image, you might want a representation that captures the objects and how they relate to each other, without being overly sensitive to a small change in lighting. But that doesn’t happen automatically just because you map the image into a vector. What ends up in that vector depends on the objective, the data, and the assumptions you build into the learning process.

r001.rationale: The response says embeddings can discard input details and that their contents depend on the learning objective, but it does not clearly state that embeddings need not perform semantic abstraction of the signal.
